title: Demonstrate an understanding of a selected business environment

lessons.title: The business and its environment
lessons.html:
Every business operates in an environment

No business operates on its own. An abattoir depends on livestock farmers, feedlots, transporters, meat inspectors, retailers, butcheries, banks and consumers. Changes outside the business, such as a drought, a disease outbreak or a rise in electricity tariffs, can quickly affect profits and jobs. Understanding the business environment helps supervisors and managers anticipate change and respond.

Three layers of the environment

LayerWhat it includesControl by the business
Micro (internal)Vision and mission, management, staff, systems, plant and equipment, financesHigh
Market (task)Customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries such as agents and transportersSome influence
Macro (external)Economic, political and legal, social, technological, environmental and international factorsLittle or none

The red meat value chain

Understanding where your business fits in the value chain is part of understanding its environment. A simplified chain is: cow-calf producers on veld, then feedlots, then auctions or direct sales, then abattoirs, then wholesalers and deboning plants, then retailers and butcheries, then consumers. By-products such as hides, offal and rendered material go into other chains, such as tanning and animal feed. Each link adds value and cost. A problem at one link, such as a foot-and-mouth disease outbreak restricting animal movements, affects the whole chain.

Stakeholders

Stakeholders are people or groups with an interest in the business: owners, employees, unions, customers, suppliers, government departments, the local community and lenders. Each has different expectations. Owners want returns; employees want fair pay and safe work; communities want jobs and no pollution; regulators want compliance. Good management balances these interests.

lessons.title: Analysing the external environment
lessons.html:
Using PESTLE

A PESTLE analysis is a simple tool for scanning the macro environment. Apply it to a South African abattoir:

  • Political: government policy on land reform, agricultural support, trade agreements, and stability.
  • Economic: interest rates, inflation, fuel and electricity prices, consumer spending power, the exchange rate affecting exports and imported inputs.
  • Social: population growth, urbanisation, changing diets, demand for halal or kosher products, concern about animal welfare.
  • Technological: automation, refrigeration technology, carcass classification equipment, traceability software.
  • Legal: the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, labour law and the OHS Act 85 of 1993.
  • Environmental: drought, water restrictions, effluent standards, waste disposal, climate change.

Market environment: competitive forces

In the market environment, consider:

  • Customers: who buys, what they want, how much bargaining power large retailers have.
  • Suppliers: availability and price of slaughter animals, packaging, chemicals.
  • Competitors: other abattoirs in the region, imported meat, alternative proteins such as chicken.
  • New entrants: how easy it is for a new abattoir to open, considering licensing and capital costs.
  • Substitutes: products customers could switch to.

Opportunities and threats

Environmental scanning should produce a list of opportunities, such as export market access or growing demand for processed products, and threats, such as disease outbreaks, load-shedding or a competitor's price cuts. Management uses these to plan, for example investing in backup generators to reduce the impact of power interruptions.

lessons.title: Internal environment and responding to change
lessons.html:
Looking inside the business

The internal environment is what the business controls. Key elements include:

  • Vision and mission: what the business aims to be and do.
  • Management and structure: who decides and how departments relate.
  • Resources: people and skills, plant and equipment, finance, information systems.
  • Business functions: production, purchasing, marketing and sales, human resources, finance, administration and public relations.
  • Culture: shared values and the way things are done.

SWOT analysis

Combining the internal and external views gives a SWOT analysis:

Strengths (internal)Weaknesses (internal)
Skilled slaughter team, good hygiene record, location near feedlotsOld refrigeration plant, high staff turnover, limited cold storage
Opportunities (external)Threats (external)
New retail contract, export certification, demand for value-added productsDisease outbreaks, drought reducing animal numbers, rising electricity costs

Strategies use strengths to take opportunities, fix weaknesses, and reduce exposure to threats.

Responding to change

When the environment changes, businesses respond by adjusting products, costs, processes or markets. For example, during a drought farmers may sell more animals, so slaughter numbers rise for a time and then fall sharply later as herds are rebuilt. A well-run abattoir plans for this by managing staff contracts, maintenance timing and cash flow.

The supervisor's role

Supervisors see changes first: lighter carcasses, more bruising from long transport, new customer specifications or staff concerns. Reporting these observations helps management respond early. Supervisors also explain changes to their teams to reduce uncertainty.

Key points

  • The business environment has micro, market and macro layers.
  • PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
  • Customers, suppliers and competitors form the market environment.
  • SWOT combines internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats.
  • Supervisors help the business respond by reporting changes they observe.
